provenance.note: Indicator text, claim wording, hypothesis verdicts and attribution, copied from the sources listed.

indicators.label: GDP per person (PPP, constant 2021 international $)
indicators.plain: How much an average person's share of the economy is worth, adjusted for local prices and for inflation.
indicators.caveats: Based on International Comparison Program price surveys; levels are revised when new rounds are published.

indicators.label: GDP growth (annual %)
indicators.plain: How much the whole economy grew (or shrank) compared with the year before.
indicators.caveats: Small economies and conflict years can show very large swings.

indicators.label: Inflation, consumer prices (annual %)
indicators.plain: How much everyday prices rose compared with a year earlier.
indicators.caveats: Extreme tails (hyperinflation) are real, not errors; handle with a documented transform.

indicators.label: Unemployment (% of labour force, modelled ILO estimate)
indicators.plain: The share of people who want a job and are looking for one but do not have one.
indicators.caveats: Modelled, not surveyed every year; definitions and survey quality differ across countries.

indicators.label: Population, total
indicators.plain: How many people live in the country.

indicators.label: Exports of goods and services (% of GDP)
indicators.plain: How much of the economy's output is sold abroad.
indicators.caveats: Small trade hubs can exceed 100% because exports include re-exported goods.

indicators.label: Gross capital formation (% of GDP)
indicators.plain: How much of the economy's output goes into building things (machines, buildings, roads) rather than being used up.
indicators.caveats: Inventory changes can make single years volatile.

indicators.label: Current account balance (% of GDP)
indicators.plain: Whether the country earns more from the rest of the world than it spends there (positive) or the reverse (negative).
indicators.caveats: Patchy coverage; sign conventions follow the IMF balance of payments manual.

indicators.label: Central government debt (% of GDP)
indicators.plain: How much the national government owes, compared with a year of the whole economy's output.
indicators.caveats: Central government only, so not comparable with general government figures; coverage is poor.

indicators.label: General government gross debt (% of GDP)
indicators.plain: How much all levels of government owe, compared with a year of the whole economy's output.
indicators.caveats: Years from the projection year onward are IMF projections and never enter headline or training tables. Some zeros (for example Macao) need review.

indicators.label: Life expectancy at birth (years)
indicators.plain: How long a newborn baby could expect to live, on average, given today's death rates.
indicators.caveats: Optional social context. UN estimates include sharp crisis-year dips (for example South Sudan 1998) and some erratic series (Central African Republic); lower bound widened from 20 to 5 on 2026-10-14 after seeing these, see docs/DECISIONS.md.

attribution: The World Bank: World Development Indicators: data sources as listed in each indicator's metadata (IMF International Financial Statistics, IMF balance of payments and government finance statistics, UN Population Division, ILO, International Comparison Program). CC BY 4.0. Retrieved 2026-10-14; reshaped, flagged and in some cases excluded by this project (docs/DATA_LOG.md). Terms: https://www.worldbank.org/ext/en/legal/terms-conditions/datasets

IMF, World Economic Outlook (October 2026), General government gross debt, via the IMF DataMapper (https://www.imf.org/external/datamapper). Values from 2026 onward are projections and are not used in analysis. Transformations are described in docs/DATA_LOG.md.
Natural Earth (when used): "Made with Natural Earth" (optional, public domain).

hypotheses.statement: Four to six stable country types exist, and resampling recovers the same groups at least 80% of the time.
hypotheses.evidence: k=4: mean ARI 0.64, silhouette 0.18 vs null 95th 0.17; k=5: mean ARI 0.57, silhouette 0.19 vs null 95th 0.16; k=6: mean ARI 0.57, silhouette 0.19 vs null 95th 0.16

hypotheses.statement: Global shock years account for a clear majority of inflation spikes.
hypotheses.evidence: 1 global shock years hold 15% of inflation-spike events (rule: more than 50%)

hypotheses.statement: Convergence of poorer economies is visible within regions but weak across the whole world.
hypotheses.evidence: 3 of 5 regions with significant convergence (Europe & Central Asia, Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan & Pakistan, Sub-Saharan Africa); global beta -0.0042 (95% -0.0061 to -0.0023) versus median regional |beta| 0.0065

hypotheses.statement: Next-year inflation is forecast no better by the best model than by repeating this year's value, in most income groups.
hypotheses.evidence: 0 of 4 groups with relative MAE at least 1; 2 with an interval entirely below 1

C1.claim: Population is observed for all 217 economies in every year 1995-2024; life expectancy for 216
C1.caveat: Population is a UN estimate; one economy has no life expectancy after an exclusion

C2.claim: GDP growth, income per person and unemployment are available for at least 84% of economies in every year; central government debt for 15-26%

C3.claim: The analysis window ends in 2024 because 2025 has 78% inflation coverage

C4.claim: Missing data is mostly whole series that never start, start late or end early; gaps inside a series are rare
C4.caveat: Counts, not causes; central government debt is the exception (36 economies with gaps)
C4.status: Checked (complete, never-reported and gap counts recomputed in SQL for all 11 indicators, `tests/test_independent_checks_m0.py`)

C5.claim: Economies with data in fewer than half the years are much smaller than the rest, and their income ranks are no lower: the effect is positive for seven of nine indicators, small and not significant for the other two, and significantly positive for unemployment
C5.caveat: Rank tests; income group is ordinal; the lacking group is small (8 to 46 economies); failing to find a difference does not prove there is none
C5.status: Checked (population effect for every indicator recomputed with a hand-written rank test, `tests/test_independent_checks_m0.py`); income effect (rank-biserial, p) and region effect (chi-square, Cramer's V) for all nine indicators recomputed by hand, `tests/test_independent_checks_p6.py`)

C6.claim: Pooling economies and years can change a correlation's sign or size; 22 of 55 pairs change sign, 4 materially
C6.caveat: Association only; intervals resample economies (200 resamples); within-economy values are driven by shared trends
C6.status: Checked (pooled Spearman and within-economy correlation of all 55 pairs and the 22 sign flips recomputed with pandas, `tests/test_independent_checks_m0.py`; interval endpoints of the five largest pairs reproduced within 0.04 by a separate bootstrap over economies, `tests/test_independent_checks_p6.py`)

C7.claim: Unusual year-on-year jumps are concentrated in 2009 and 2020-2022 (at least 1.5 times an average year)
C7.caveat: Threshold (median + 10 MAD) is a choice; shown under two versions of the rule; a count, not a test of shock synchrony (that is M2)
C7.status: Checked (warnings per year recomputed in SQL for all 11 indicators, `tests/test_independent_checks_m0.py`)

C10.claim: Using seven features in 2015-19, k-means groups beat a null made by shuffling each feature only slightly (silhouette 0.18 to 0.19 for four to six groups against a 95th percentile of 0.16 to 0.17), and beat a correlated normal cloud with the data's covariance by 0.01 to 0.02 (95th percentile 0.17 to 0.18)
C10.caveat: Weak structure by the usual silhouette reading (below 0.25). Four to six groups were tried with no adjustment for the search. Shuffling columns removes the correlations between features, so beating it does not separate discrete groups from a continuum. The correlated-normal null was added after the outside review; staying above it fits weak structure or non-normal data and does not show clusters
C10.status: Checked (silhouette recomputed by hand in `tests/test_independent_checks.py`; the permutation null reproduced with a separate k-means run: 95th percentile within 0.012; the correlated-normal null reproduced with a separate run, `tests/test_independent_checks_p6.py`)

C11.claim: The groups are not stable: mean ARI is 0.57 to 0.64 for k = 4 to 6, below the 0.80 bar, so hypothesis H1 is rejected
C11.caveat: 163 economies with complete data; 200 resamples of economies; one feature set and scaling; z-score scaling, imputed economies and three other seeds all give mean ARI of 0.52 to 0.70, still below 0.80 (`outputs/m1/extra_sensitivity.csv`)
C11.status: Checked (reproduced in 15 variant runs, all below 0.80)

C12.claim: At k = 5 about half of the 163 economies are core members (91, or 56%, in the main run); one of five groups has none
C12.caveat: Core means same group in at least 80% of resamples after matching groups
C12.status: Checked (core share reproduced under three other seeds, within 12 points of the main run, `tests/test_independent_checks_m0.py`)

C13.claim: Agreement between consecutive five-year windows (ARI 0.04 to 0.42) is lower than agreement between resamples within one window (about 0.57), but the two are not like for like, so how much of the gap is real change is not known
C13.caveat: Complete-case samples differ by window (82 to 164 economies), and a resample of one window is a different perturbation from a new window; descriptive only
C13.status: Checked (adjusted Rand index recomputed by hand, `tests/test_independent_checks_p3.py`)

C14.claim: Economies left out of the 2015-19 clustering for missing data are much smaller than those kept (and somewhat higher in income group)
C14.status: Checked (rank-biserial effect and group size recomputed with a hand-written rank test, `tests/test_independent_checks_p3.py`)

C15.claim: Under the pre-registered definition only 2008 is a global shock year for inflation spikes, holding 15% of 88 events, so hypothesis H2 is rejected
C15.caveat: Thresholds are arbitrary; 1,000 shuffles; Holm across 29 years; annual data; the verdict holds under five seeds (share 15% to 36%); the test assumes the years open to an economy are exchangeable. With 10,000 shuffles 1999 and 2022 are also global years and hold 36% together with 2008 (C32), still short of a majority
C15.status: Checked for the event catalogue (recomputed in SQL; 88 events, 13 in 2008); the shuffle test was reimplemented with separate random numbers and finds 2008 every time, `tests/test_independent_checks_p6.py`). Borderline years are seed-dependent and documented, as in C17

C16.claim: H2 is rejected under loose (39% in global years 2008 and 2022) and tight (none) definitions too
C16.caveat: Which years count as global depends on the thresholds
C16.status: Checked for the event sets (all three threshold sets recomputed in SQL, `tests/test_independent_checks_p3.py`); the shuffle test on loose and tight thresholds was reimplemented and gives the same global years (2008 and 2022; none) and the 39% share, `tests/test_independent_checks_p6.py`)

C17.claim: Recessions cluster in 2009 and 2020 and debt jumps in 1998, 2009 and 2020, far above a shuffled-years null
C17.caveat: With 1,000 shuffles and 29 tested years the smallest adjusted p the test can give is about 0.029; clustering in time does not show a common cause; borderline years (1999, 2022, 1998 for debt) change with the shuffle seed
C17.status: Checked for the event sets (recomputed in SQL, `tests/test_independent_checks_p3.py`); the shuffle test was reimplemented and finds 2009 and 2020 for recessions and debt jumps every time, `tests/test_independent_checks_p6.py`); core years also reproduced under five seeds in M2. 1998 and 1999 are borderline

C18.claim: A third or fewer of inflation spikes and recessions, and about 70% of debt jumps, have a detected change in the economy's average level (PELT) within one year
C18.caveat: Descriptive; penalty finds many change points in volatile series
C18.status: Checked (overlap recomputed from the saved event and change-point tables, `tests/test_independent_checks_m0.py`); the change-point finder was tested against an exhaustive search on 12 random series, `tests/test_m2.py`; the saved change-point tables themselves were not recomputed separately)

C19.claim: Over 1995-2024 lower-income economies grew modestly faster: slope -0.42 (95% interval -0.61 to -0.23) points of growth per log unit of starting income, 187 economies
C19.caveat: Descriptive regression, no controls; measurement error in starting income biases towards convergence (the slope is unchanged when four years are averaged at each end)
C19.status: Checked (slope and sample size recomputed in SQL, `tests/test_independent_checks.py`)

C20.claim: Convergence is period-dependent: strong in 2005-2014 (-0.81) and indistinguishable from zero in 2015-2024 (-0.04, interval includes zero) for all economies
C20.caveat: Different samples by period (188 to 197 economies)
C20.status: Checked (all four period slopes and sample sizes recomputed in SQL, `tests/test_independent_checks_p3.py`)

C21.claim: H3 is confirmed under its pre-registered rule but is fragile: it flips to rejected if the lowest 5% of starting incomes are dropped, and only one region survives Holm correction
C21.caveat: Rule uses unadjusted 95% intervals; five regional tests; flips to rejected under two of three sensitivity variants (poorest 5% dropped; four-year averages)
C21.status: Checked for the regional slopes (recomputed in SQL, `tests/test_independent_checks_p3.py`); HC3 interval code tested against the closed form; all four sensitivity variants (sample size, global slope and interval, regions significant, verdict) and the Holm result (only Europe and Central Asia survives) recomputed with separate code, `tests/test_independent_checks_p6.py`)

C22.claim: The spread of log income across economies narrowed only slightly (1.21 to 1.16), flat until about 2005 and widening again after 2020
C22.caveat: Economies with data change by year; balanced-sample trend is the same
C22.status: Checked (series and trend recomputed in SQL, `tests/test_independent_checks_p3.py`)

C24.claim: For inflation the best model (LightGBM, level) has about 7% lower error than persistence (MAE 0.642 against 0.691 on the asinh scale; relative MAE 0.929, 95% interval 0.904 to 0.958), 2005-2024
C24.caveat: Hindsight choice of best model favours it; asinh scale; 3,659 forecasts
C24.status: Checked (persistence MAE and sample size recomputed in SQL; relative MAE recomputed by hand, `tests/test_m5_independent.py`)

C25.claim: The per-economy AR(1), not persistence, is the strongest simple inflation baseline (0.657 against 0.691)
C25.caveat: Common-support comparison; AR(1) coefficient clipped to [-1, 1]
C25.status: Checked (persistence recomputed in SQL; AR(1) code tested against a hand formula in `tests/test_m5.py`)

C26.claim: For growth the trailing 5-year mean is the strongest baseline (MAE 3.47) and no learned model beats it (best: Ridge change, 3.52); all are about 11% better than persistence (3.97)
C26.caveat: 4,151 forecasts; learned models tested are a short list
C26.status: Checked (persistence and trailing-mean MAE recomputed in SQL)

C27.claim: H5 is inconclusive: the best inflation model has lower error than persistence in all four income groups but the interval is clearly below 1 in only two
C27.caveat: Verdict identical in all scopes, including a post hoc scope that drops the 16 forecast rows touching values below -5%, and under three other bootstrap seeds
C27.status: Checked (reproduced under other seeds; group ratios from saved predictions)

C28.claim: The 90% intervals cover 86% to 88% overall and only 77% to 81% for growth in 2020-2024
C28.caveat: Intervals exist for 2008 onward; calibration lags shocks
C28.status: Checked (coverage recomputed from the saved intervals)

C29.claim: Of the 16 World Bank inflation values below -5% that have an IMF counterpart, 7 agree, 3 have the same sign with a 2 to 4 point gap, and 6 are strongly contradicted (the IMF shows 1% to 31% where the World Bank shows -7% to -17%)
C29.caveat: Only values below -5% were checked, not every inflation value; read in Chrome from IMF DataMapper PCPIPCH (WEO October 2026); one value (Iraq 1996) has no IMF figure
C29.status: Checked (second source read; every World Bank value in the file tested against the panel, `tests/test_m5_independent.py`)

C30.claim: Both targets' models depend mainly on the economy's own recent history: refitting without it raises held-out error by about 17% to 18%; for growth, log income per person is the second most important feature
C30.caveat: Describes the models, not the economy; partial-dependence slopes (inflation about 0.4 per unit of the latest value; growth about 0.3, and about -0.8 per log unit of income) are averages over the 5th to 95th percentile
C30.status: Checked (an ablation refit, a different method from permutation importance, gives the same conclusion, `tests/test_m5_independent.py`)

C31.claim: If the model is chosen each year from earlier test years' errors instead of in hindsight (from 2008, the method with the lowest error so far among all eight), inflation error is 0.746 against 0.721 for persistence on the same rows (ratio 1.03, 95% interval 1.00 to 1.07), while the hindsight winner scores 0.666; for growth the rule scores 3.92 against 3.60 for the trailing mean and 4.18 for persistence
C31.caveat: Post hoc, added after the outside review; one simple rule, which does not show that no selection rule could work; 3,101 inflation and 3,519 growth forecasts; the choice among close methods is noisy; no untouched data remain for a confirmatory test
C31.status: Checked (the rule reimplemented in plain pandas, `tests/test_independent_checks_p6.py`)

C32.claim: With 10,000 shuffles instead of 1,000, three years are global for inflation spikes (1999, 2008, 2022) and hold 36% of the 88 events, so H2 is still rejected; debt jumps keep their three global years (1998, 2009, 2020) and recessions gain 2012 narrowly (adjusted p 0.049)
C32.caveat: Post hoc resolution check (exceedances of 10, 0 and 9 in 10,000 shuffles for 1999, 2008 and 2022; Monte Carlo standard error of p about 0.0003); the pre-registered result (1,000 shuffles, seed 42) is unchanged and stays the verdict; adjusted p for 1999 and 2022 is 0.03 to 0.04 in two runs and for recession 2012 about 0.05, so these years sit close to the cut-off
C32.status: Checked (the shuffle test reimplemented with separate random numbers at 10,000 shuffles, `tests/test_independent_checks_p6.py`)

C34.claim: Four series hold exact zeros in the raw files that were excluded as missing values: Venezuela's exports and capital formation (1995 to 2011), Ethiopia's capital formation (1995 to 2010) and the Republic of Congo's general government debt (1995 to 1999). Each is followed by non-zero values and the panel holds missing values for those years
C34.caveat: That the zeros are placeholders and not real values is a judgement from the pattern; no second source was read for Congo or the two World Bank series
C34.status: Checked (the raw World Bank and IMF files read directly, `tests/test_independent_checks_p6.py`)
